q: On the stress-strain diagram of mild steel shown, which point is the elastic limit, the highest stress from which the bar still returns to its original length when unloaded?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Point B, the elastic limit, sits just above the proportional limit (A). Between A and B the curve is no longer straight, but unloading still leaves no permanent set. Past B the steel yields (C) and some deformation stays.

q: Which formula gives the uniform normal stress in a member carrying an axial load P over a cross-sectional area A?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Normal stress is force per unit area, σ = P/A, in N/mm² (MPa) or kPa. It is uniform only when the load passes through the centroid of the section.

q: On the stress-strain diagram of mild steel shown, which point marks the yield point, where the bar stretches markedly with little or no increase in stress?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Point C is the yield point. Mild steel shows a flat yield plateau there: strain grows a lot while stress stays about the same. The yield stress Fy (such as 275 MPa for Grade 40 bars) is the value design codes use.

q: What is the strain energy per unit volume a material can absorb without any permanent deformation?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: The modulus of resilience is the area under the stress-strain curve up to the elastic (proportional) limit, about Fy²/2E. The modulus of toughness is the whole area up to fracture, so it is always larger.

q: What is the geometric center of a plane area, which coincides with the center of mass when the density is uniform?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: The centroid is the average position of the area. Bending stresses are measured from the neutral axis, which passes through the centroid. The shear center is a different point, where a load causes bending without twisting.

q: In which range of the stress-strain curve does a permanent deformation remain after the load is removed?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Beyond the elastic limit the material is in the plastic range: atoms slip past each other and do not return, so unloading leaves a permanent set. In the elastic range every deformation is recovered.

q: On the stress-strain diagram of mild steel shown, which point is the proportional limit, the end of the straight-line part of the curve?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Point A ends the straight line from the origin. Up to A, stress is proportional to strain and Hooke's law holds; the slope of that line is the modulus of elasticity E.

q: What kind of stress develops in a member loaded by a force acting along its longitudinal axis?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: An axial force acts perpendicular to the cross-section, so it produces normal stress, σ = P/A: tension if it pulls, compression if it pushes. Shear stress comes from forces parallel to the section.

q: What twisting action about a member's longitudinal axis produces shear stress across its cross-section?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Torsion (torque) twists a member such as a shaft or a spandrel beam. It causes shear stress that is zero at the center and greatest at the outer surface, τ = Tc/J for a round shaft.

q: Which formula locates the centroid ȳ of a composite area made of simple parts?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Split the shape into simple parts, multiply each area by the distance of its own centroid from a reference axis, add these moments, and divide by the total area. The same rule with x gives x̄.

q: What property lets a material undergo large plastic deformation in tension before it breaks?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Ductility is stretching in tension, as when steel is drawn into wire. Malleability is the similar ability under compression, such as rolling or hammering. Brittle materials like cast iron and plain concrete break with little warning.

q: What is the deformation that remains in a material after the load is removed?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Permanent set is the leftover inelastic strain once a material has been loaded past its elastic limit. Elastic deformation, by contrast, disappears completely on unloading.

q: Which formula locates the centroid x̄ of a composite area made of simple parts?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: The x-centroid is the area-weighted average of each part's x-distance: add every Aᵢxᵢ and divide by the total area ΣAᵢ.

q: What internal action pulls or stretches a member, making it longer?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Tension elongates a member, as in a hanger rod or the bottom chord of a truss. Its opposite, compression, shortens it.

q: What is the progressive failure of a material under repeated cycles of stress, often at stresses below its static strength?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Fatigue cracks start at small flaws and grow a little with each load cycle until the member snaps. It matters for crane girders, bridges and machine supports. Creep and relaxation are time effects under a steady load, not cycling.

q: Some normally ductile materials behave in a more brittle way when loaded very quickly. What is this effect called?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: The strain-rate effect: at high loading rates, such as impact or blast, the material has less time to yield, so its strength goes up but its ductility can go down.

q: Which ratio defines Young's modulus (the modulus of elasticity), E?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: E = σ/ε in the linear-elastic range, the slope of the straight part of the stress-strain curve. Steel is about 200,000 MPa. Shear stress over shear strain is the shear modulus G, and lateral over axial strain is Poisson's ratio.

q: Which internal action produces tension on one face and compression on the opposite face of a member?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: A bending moment curves the member: fibres on one side stretch and on the other side shorten, with zero stress at the neutral axis. In a simple beam under gravity load, the bottom is in tension and the top in compression.

q: What is the gradual drop in stress over time in a material held at a constant strain?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Stress relaxation is the loss of stress at a fixed length, for example the slow loss of force in prestressing tendons. Creep is the mirror case: strain grows over time under a constant stress.

q: What internal action shortens a member by pushing its particles together?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Compression shortens a member, as in columns, struts and the top chord of a truss. Slender members in compression can buckle long before the material crushes.

q: What type of deformation disappears completely once the load is removed?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Elastic deformation is fully recoverable because the atoms only stretch their bonds and do not slip. Plastic deformation and permanent set remain after unloading.

q: A 100 kN axial force acts on a cross-section of 2,000 mm². What uniform normal stress results?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
steps: Convert the load to newtons: P = 100 kN = 100,000 N

q: How does low temperature typically affect steel and some other metals?
o: It removes the yield plateau and raises ductility
It lowers ductility and can make them fracture in a brittle way
It has no effect on how they fail
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Below a transition temperature many steels lose toughness and can crack suddenly with little deformation, the cause of well-known ship and bridge failures. Heat has the opposite effect: it lowers strength and stiffness.

q: What is a force that acts along the longitudinal axis of a member called?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: An axial force acts along the member's centroidal axis and causes uniform tension or compression. A shear force acts across the member, a moment bends it, and a torque twists it.

q: What is the slow increase in deformation of a material under a load that is held constant over a long time?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Under sustained load, concrete and timber keep deflecting for years; this is creep. It is why long-term deflections of concrete beams can be two to three times the immediate ones.

q: What is the total strain energy per unit volume a material absorbs up to fracture?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: The modulus of toughness is the whole area under the stress-strain curve up to rupture. Ductile steel has a large one because it stretches a long way before breaking. The modulus of resilience only counts the elastic part.

q: Which instrument measures the small changes in length of a test specimen so that strain can be computed?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: An extensometer is clamped to the specimen over a known gauge length and reads its elongation, so strain ε = ΔL/L can be found. The testing machine itself reads the load.

q: A 2,000 mm gauge length elongates by 2 mm under load. What engineering strain results?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: ε = ΔL/L₀ = 2 mm / 2,000 mm = 0.001. Strain has no units because it is length over length.

q: On the stress-strain diagram of mild steel shown, which point marks the ultimate tensile strength?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Point D is the peak of the curve, the ultimate (tensile) strength: the highest engineering stress the bar reaches. After D the bar necks, the load it can carry drops, and it breaks at E.

q: In which range of the stress-strain curve does a material return to its original dimensions when unloaded?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: The elastic range runs from zero up to the elastic limit. In it, unloading retraces the curve back to zero strain. Past that point the material enters the plastic range.

q: What is a stress trajectory?
o: A line whose length shows the size of the stress
The path a crack follows after fracture
A line showing the direction of the principal stresses at each point
The curve of stress against time
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Stress trajectories are drawn so that at every point they point along a principal stress direction. They show direction only, not magnitude. In a beam, the tension trajectories explain why diagonal cracks form near the supports.

q: What property lets a material be plastically deformed by compression, such as rolling or hammering, without cracking?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Malleability is shaping under compression: gold can be beaten into leaf and steel rolled into plate. Ductility is the matching ability in tension, such as drawing into wire.

q: What deformation makes layers of a material slide past each other under forces acting parallel to a plane?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Shear stress acts along a plane, and shear deformation changes angles rather than lengths. Examples are bolts in a lap joint and the web of a beam near its supports.

q: Which branch of mechanics deals with the internal stresses and deformations that forces produce in structural members?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Statics treats bodies as rigid and finds the external forces and reactions. Strength of materials (mechanics of materials) takes those forces and finds the internal stresses, strains and deflections.

q: Which formula defines the shear modulus (modulus of rigidity), G?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: G is shear stress τ divided by shear strain γ in the elastic range. For steel it is about 77,000 to 80,000 MPa. It is linked to E by G = E / 2(1 + ν).

q: Why does strain have no unit?
o: It is always expressed as a percentage of stress
It is force divided by area
It is measured only in the elastic range
It is a change in length divided by an original length
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Strain ε = ΔL/L₀ is length over length, so the units cancel. It is often written as mm/mm, as a percentage, or in microstrain (×10⁻⁶).

q: Which law states that, within the elastic range, stress is proportional to strain?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Hooke's law, σ = Eε, holds up to the proportional limit. The constant of proportionality is the modulus of elasticity E.

q: What is the ratio of lateral strain to axial strain in a member under uniaxial load?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: When a bar is stretched it also gets thinner. Poisson's ratio ν is the size of that lateral strain divided by the axial strain: about 0.3 for steel and 0.15 to 0.2 for concrete.

q: What is the general ability of a material to absorb energy before it fractures?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: A tough material both resists stress and deforms a lot before breaking, so it soaks up energy. Resilience is energy absorbed only in the elastic range; stiffness is resistance to deformation, measured by E.

q: What is the ability of a material to recover its original shape when the load is removed?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Elasticity is recovery of shape after unloading, valid up to the elastic limit. Plasticity is the opposite: deformation that stays.

q: Which formula gives normal (engineering) strain?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Engineering strain is the change in length divided by the original length. From Hooke's law, it can also be found as ε = σ/E in the elastic range.

q: Shear stress divided by shear strain gives which elastic constant?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: τ/γ is the shear modulus G. Normal stress over normal strain is Young's modulus E, and volumetric stress over volumetric strain is the bulk modulus K. It is a common mix-up to call τ/γ "E".

q: On the stress-strain diagram of mild steel shown, which point marks the rupture (breaking) strength?
ref: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials; Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials
n: Point E is where the bar fractures. On an engineering curve it sits below the ultimate strength D because the neck has shrunk the real area, so a smaller load breaks it.
